h1:
Things to Do in Nan
Temples, Mountains & Old Town
intro: Nan is a town you take slowly. In town you can spend a whole day visiting old temples, looking at the mural paintings, and drinking coffee around the old quarter. Head out of town and you run into high mountains, seas of mist, and roads that curve through the valleys. We've pulled together the Nan spots that made us understand why people keep coming back, sorted into temples in town, mountains and nature, and the easy-walking old quarter.

blocks.html: Nan gives you two trips in one. Spend the first half-day walking the old town, visiting temples, looking at centuries-old murals, then sit with a coffee by the road in the evening. Spend the other half driving out toward Pua–Bo Kluea, where you'll find Doi Phu Kha, the mist, and the winding road that plenty of people come specifically to drive. We'll group the sights so you get the big picture first, then go through each one.

Nan's town temples sit close together, all within walking distance, so you can visit three or four in a single morning. The draw is the Lanna–Tai Lue architecture and murals you won't easily find elsewhere.

items.name: Wat Phumin
items.blurb: A cruciform-style temple in the heart of the old town, famous for its 'Pu Man Ya Man' mural — the whispering-lovers painting that has become a symbol of Nan. The walls tell the everyday life of old Nan in fine detail. It's the first temple most people stop at.

items.name: Wat Phra That Chae Haeng
items.blurb: Nan's guardian stupa — a gold-clad chedi set on a rise across the river. It's the year-of-the-Rabbit stupa and locals hold it in high regard. It sits just outside the old town, about a 10-minute drive or ride away.
items.meta: ~3 km from the old town · no entry fee

items.name: Wat Phra That Khao Noi
items.blurb: Up on a hilltop on the western side of town, with a large standing Buddha and a viewpoint terrace that takes in all of Nan. It's a popular spot for sunset, and you can drive right up to the car park.
items.meta: Nan town viewpoint · drivable to the top

items.name: Wat Sri Mongkol (Kong)
items.blurb: An old temple around Tha Wang Pha district, with a back terrace looking out over green rice fields with the Doi Phu Kha range behind. A good photo stop on the way up to Pua.
items.meta: Tha Wang Pha district · rice-field & Doi Phu Kha view

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.html: The old-town temples are all walkable from each other. Park near Wat Phumin and just walk between them. Go early and it's cooler and quieter than mid-morning.

The other half of Nan's appeal is out of town. The Pua–Bo Kluea route climbs up to Doi Phu Kha, passing villages tucked in the valleys, while down south around Na Noi you'll find Doi Samer Dao and the unusual earth pillars. These spots are far from town, so plan your driving time carefully.

items.name: Doi Phu Kha National Park
items.blurb: Nan's highest mountain, with the km-1715 viewpoint where you can watch a sea of mist fill the valleys on cold-season mornings. It's home to the Chompoo Phu Kha trees that bloom pink early in the year, and the air stays cool almost year-round.
items.meta: Pua district · park entry around 20–40 THB

items.name: Doi Samer Dao
items.blurb: Inside Sri Nan National Park in Na Noi district, this broad ridge gives a 360-degree view — stargazing at night, mist and sunrise in the morning. It's a popular camping spot, so book a place ahead in the cold season.

items.name: Bo Kluea Rock Salt
items.blurb: A mountain salt-making site that still boils salt the old way — rare to see in Thailand. You can walk through the salt-boiling process and buy salt and local products from the community. It's a hands-on look at local life unlike anywhere else.

items.name: Ban Sapan
items.blurb: A small village in a valley near Bo Kluea, with a stream, terraced rice fields, and riverside cafes. The mood is quiet and slow, and people like to stay a night at a homestay to wake up to the mist.

items.name: Sao Din Na Noi (Hom Chom)
items.blurb: Oddly shaped earth pillars carved by water and wind over millions of years. There's a short walking trail to take it in, and it's near Doi Samer Dao, so you can pair them in one trip.
items.meta: Na Noi district · near Doi Samer Dao

blocks.title: Tip
blocks.html: Clear mist at Doi Phu Kha and Doi Samer Dao usually comes in the cold season (Nov–Feb), early in the morning. In the rainy season the mountain roads get slick and mist sits all day. Allow extra driving time and check the weather before you go.

blocks.text: The sky road and scenic drives

blocks.html: Route 1256 along the Pua–Bo Kluea stretch is the road many people come specifically to drive. It runs along the ridgelines, and in places it feels like you're floating above the mist, which is why it's called the 'sky road.' It's an easy, enjoyable drive with several viewpoints and cafes to stop at along the way.

items.name: Route 1256 Sky Road (Pua–Bo Kluea)
items.blurb: A winding ridgeline road. The most popular photo spot is where the road shoots straight toward the mountains. Drive it in the morning for a chance at mist. It actually takes longer than the distance suggests because of all the curves.

items.name: Kiew Muang Viewpoint (The View)
items.blurb: A roadside cafe and viewpoint around Pua, looking out over a wide sweep of valley. A good place to pause for a coffee on the way up to Bo Kluea.

items.name: Doi Sakad
items.blurb: A mountain village in Pua district, about 22 km from Pua town, with terraced-field views and small cafes. The road up is steep, so drive carefully.

blocks.text: Nan old town and food along the walk

blocks.html: Nan's old town is compact and easy to explore on foot — no car needed. Around it are museums, coffee shops, and an evening market to stop at. On Friday to Sunday evenings there's the Kad Khuang Mueang walking street where you can graze on local food.

items: Nan National Museum — once the residence of Nan's ruling lords, it displays the city's prized black elephant tusk. Out front, the arched lamduan (frangipani) trees make a classic photo spot.
Kad Khuang Mueang walking street — open Friday to Sunday evenings on the square in front of Wat Phumin, with local food and crafts and a relaxed vibe.
Old-town cafes — Nan has small coffee shops in old buildings scattered across town, good for a rest between temple visits.
Woven cloth and preserved mafai — Nan is known for Tai Lue woven textiles and candied mafai (Burmese grape). You can pick them up at souvenir shops around town.

blocks.title: Best time to go
blocks.html: The cold season (Nov–Feb) is Nan's high season — cool air and clear mist — but accommodation fills up fast and prices climb. To avoid the crowds, try the late-rainy/early-cold window, when the rice fields are still green and there are fewer people.

faq.q: What are the must-see places in Nan?
faq.a: In town: Wat Phumin with its whispering-lovers mural, Phra That Chae Haeng, and Phra That Khao Noi for the town view. Out of town: Doi Phu Kha, Doi Samer Dao, Bo Kluea, Ban Sapan, and the Route 1256 sky road on the Pua–Bo Kluea stretch.

faq.q: How many days do you need in Nan?
faq.a: If you're only doing the town and temples, 1–2 days is enough. But if you want to head up to Pua, Bo Kluea, and Doi Phu Kha too, allow 3 days and 2 nights, because the mountain roads are slow and the sights are far apart.

faq.q: When is the best time to visit Nan?
faq.a: The cold season, November through February, is when the air is cool and you have the best chance of clear mist. But it's crowded and accommodation books up fast. If you want to skip the crowds, try the late-rainy/early-cold window, when the rice fields are still green.

faq.q: Is the Route 1256 sky road hard to drive?
faq.a: It's a well-paved road but with lots of curves and climbs. Drive it during the day, fill up on fuel before you head up, and avoid driving at night or in the rainy season when the road is slick and the mist comes down.

faq.q: How far are Nan's out-of-town sights?
faq.a: Pua is about 60 km from Nan town, with Bo Kluea and Sapan another 50 km or so beyond. Doi Samer Dao and Sao Din are down south around Na Noi, the opposite direction from Pua, so it's best to split the northern and southern sights into separate days.
